title: pg
text: A PostgreSQL client, written in slang over net . A query waiting on the server parks its task like any socket read, so unlike sql it does not block a worker thread: a server can hold many database connections on a handful of threads. Errors keep the server's own text and SQLSTATE, through the same result[_, str] story as every other package. slang Copy import "pg" ; import "time" ; import "log" ; let dl = until_of (time. mono () + 5000000000 ); let pr = pg. new_pool ( "postgres://app:secret@db.internal/shop" , 10 ); guard let pool = pr else let e = err_of (pr) { log. error ( "db url: " + e); exit ( 1 ); } let r = pg. pool_query (pool, "SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price < $1 ORDER BY id" , [pg. arg_float ( 20.0 )], dl); guard let rows = r else let e = err_of (r) { log. error ( "query: " + e); // ERROR: relation "products" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01) exit ( 1 ); } let i = 0 ; while i < rows.count { println ( to_str (pg. get_int (rows, i, 0 )) + " " + pg. get_text (rows, i, 1 )); i = i + 1 ; } Every call that talks to the server takes a deadline ( until ), like httpc ; until_of(0) waits indefinitely. For connect it covers the whole connection: DNS lookup, TCP connect, TLS handshake and login. Function Signature pg.connect(url, deadline) result[Conn, str] pg.parse_url(url) / pg.connect_config(cfg, deadline) result[Config, str] / result[Conn, str] pg.query(c, sql, args, deadline) result[Rows, str] — one statement, $1 , $2 … parameters pg.exec(c, sql, deadline) result[int, str] — several ; -separated statements, no parameters; rows affected by the last pg.close(c) — sends Terminate and closes pg.usable(c) / pg.in_transaction(c) bool pg.server_param(c, name) opt[str] — server_version , TimeZone , … pg.sqlstate(e) str — the SQLSTATE in an error, or "" if it did not come from the server Parameters travel separately from the SQL text, so a value can never be parsed as SQL, whatever it contains. Build them with pg.arg_text(s) , arg_int(n) , arg_float(x) (sent exactly, not rounded), arg_bool(b) , arg_bytes(b) (binary, for bytea ), arg_time(t) (a timez.Time , for timestamptz ; Postgres keeps microseconds) and arg_null() . A query with none takes [] . Results from query are buffered whole in a Rows (for one too big for that, see Streaming ): rows.count , rows.columns (names), rows.affected (from the command tag, so an INSERT or UPDATE through query reports its row count) and rows.tag . Read cells by row and column index; pg.col(rows, "name") finds an index. Getter Reads pg.get_text(rows, r, c) any column, in Postgres's text form (dates, numeric , uuid , json ) pg.get_int(rows, r, c) int2 , int4 , int8 , oid , and a whole-number numeric (what sum() of an integer column returns) pg.get_float(rows, r, c) float4 , float8 , numeric , the integer types pg.get_bool(rows, r, c) bool pg.get_bytes(rows, r, c) bytea pg.get_time(rows, r, c) timestamptz as a timez.Time ( result : err for infinity or a BC date); a timestamp without a zone is read as UTC pg.get_decimal(rows, r, c) numeric and the integer types as an exact decimal.Decimal , at Postgres's scale ( result : err for NaN, infinity or more than 38 digits) pg.is_null(rows, r, c) whether the cell is NULL The getters panic on NULL, on a column of a type they do not read, on an unknown column name and on an index out of range, with a message naming the column ( column 'email' is NULL in row 3; check pg.is_null before pg.get_text ). Those are disagreements between the query and the code reading it — bugs to see, not conditions to handle — and inventing a 0 or "" would hide them. A nullable column is checked with is_null first. Like sqlx's get , not Go's Scan . pg.rows_as[T](rows) -> result[[T], str] binds columns by exact field name and decodes directly into value or gc structs, without rendering rows as JSON. Annotate

title: proc
text: Graceful shutdown and environment variables. proc.shutdown_requested() turns true once the process receives SIGTERM or SIGINT ; a blocked net.accept() / net.recv() / net.dial() is interrupted the instant the signal arrives (an err result, not a hang), so a listener loop notices without needing select or a timeout. Handling the signals is opt-in by use. A program that calls proc.shutdown_requested() anywhere — in its own code or in a package it imports — takes them over: the first SIGTERM or SIGINT only sets the flag, and a second one ends the process the way the signal would have, so a drain that never finishes cannot make it unkillable. A program that never asks keeps the default action: the signal ends it, whether or not it imports proc for anything else ( proc.getenv , say). proc.active_tasks() counts currently-running spawn ed tasks. proc.wait_idle() parks until that count is zero, so a shutting-down program can drain in-flight work without polling. Called from a spawned task, neither counts the caller (nor, for wait_idle , other tasks also waiting in it), so a task can drain the rest without waiting for itself; every test under slangc test is such a task. slang Copy import "net" ; import "proc" ; import "time" ; fn accept_and_serve (lfd: i32 ) { let ar: result [ i32 , str ] = net. accept (lfd); guard let cfd = ar else { return ; } // interrupted, or a real error spawn serve (cfd); } let lr: result [ i32 , str ] = net. listen ( 8080 ); guard let lfd = lr else { exit ( 1 ); } while !proc. shutdown_requested () { accept_and_serve (lfd); } proc. wait_idle (); proc.getenv(name) reads an environment variable, returning opt[str] ( none if unset). proc.args() is the process argument list ( [str] ); args[0] is the executable path. To parse options out of it, see flags . proc.cwd() is the working directory as result[str, str] . API # proc. shutdown_requested () -> bool # proc. active_tasks () -> int # proc. wait_idle () # proc. getenv ( str ) -> opt [ str ] # proc. args () -> [ str ] # proc. cwd () -> result [ str , str ] # proc. spawn ([ str ], [ str ], str , int ) -> result [ int , str ] # proc. kill ( int , int ) -> result [ bool , str ] # proc. wait ( int , until ) -> result [ int , str ] #

title: rand
text: Seeded, non-cryptographic random numbers for tests, simulations, sampling and retry jitter. One seed fixes the whole sequence on every platform, so a test that draws random inputs fails the same way on CI and on a laptop. slang Copy import "rand" ; let r = rand. new ( 42 ); // same seed, same sequence rand. below (r, 10 ); // int in [0, 10) rand. between (r, 1 , 6 ); // int in [1, 6], ends included rand. unit (r); // float in [0, 1) rand. chance (r, 0.25 ); // true about one time in four rand. shuffle (r, xs); // reorders xs in place rand. pick (r, xs) ?? fallback; // none when xs is empty // retry number `attempt` (0 first): uniform in [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)] time. sleep (rand. backoff (r, attempt, 100000000 , 30000000000 )); rand. jitter (r, 60000000000 , 0.1 ); // 60s, give or take 10% The generator is xoshiro256** , seeded through splitmix64 . The tests pin its exact outputs against the authors' C code, so a seed means the same sequence in every slang release. Draws are unbiased: below and between redraw rather than take a plain modulo, and between covers the full int range. below(r, 0) and between(r, 5, 1) panic, like an index out of range, since there is no value to return. backoff uses full jitter, which spreads clients that failed together across the whole interval, and saturates at cap rather than overflowing. An Rng is not locked: give each spawned task its own with rand.fork(r) , which stays reproducible from the parent's seed. rand.from_os() seeds from the OS when runs should differ. Neither is for secrets: tokens, keys and salts come from crypto.rand , because this generator's outputs reveal its state. API # gc struct Rng stdlib/rand/rand.sl:33 # A random number generator. Make one with new or from_os . fn new (seed: int ) -> Rng stdlib/rand/rand.sl:42 # A generator whose sequence is fixed by seed . Every int is a good seed, 0 and -1 included: splitmix64 spreads it over all 256 bits of state. fn from_os () -> result [Rng, str ] stdlib/rand/rand.sl:57 # A generator seeded from the operating system's CSPRNG, for when runs should differ (load generators, sampling in production). Its outputs are still predictable from earlier ones: this is not a source of secrets. fn fork (r: Rng) -> Rng stdlib/rand/rand.sl:76 # A new generator seeded from r , for handing to a spawned task. Seeded parents give seeded children, so a whole run still replays from one seed. r advances by one step. fn next_u64 (r: Rng) -> u64 stdlib/rand/rand.sl:81 # The next 64 random bits. fn below (r: Rng, n: int ) -> int stdlib/rand/rand.sl:95 # An int in [0, n), each value equally likely. Panics if n is not positive: there is no int to return, as with an index out of range. fn between (r: Rng, lo: int , hi: int ) -> int stdlib/rand/rand.sl:104 # An int in [lo, hi], both ends included, each value equally likely. Panics if lo > hi. The full range, between(r, MIN, MAX), works. fn unit (r: Rng) -> float stdlib/rand/rand.sl:119 # A float in the unit interval [0, 1): one of 2^53 evenly spaced values, so every float it returns is exact and 1.0 never appears. fn chance (r: Rng, p: float ) -> bool stdlib/rand/rand.sl:125 # True with probability p . p at or below 0 (or NaN) is never, p at or above 1 is always. fn shuffle[T](r: Rng, xs: [T]) stdlib/rand/rand.sl:136 # Reorders xs in place, every order equally likely (Fisher-Yates). fn pick[T](r: Rng, xs: [T]) -> opt [T] stdlib/rand/rand.sl:148 # One element of xs , each equally likely; none if xs is empty. fn backoff (r: Rng, attempt: int , base: int , cap: int ) -> int stdlib/rand/rand.sl:161 # How long to wait before retry number attempt (0 for the first retry): a uniform draw from [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)], the "full jitter" strategy. Spreading over the whole interval, not just its top, is what stops a crowd of clients that failed together from retrying together. Units are whatever base and cap use, nanoseconds for a durati

title: redis
text: A Redis client, written in slang over net like pg : commands waiting on the server park the task on the reactor instead of blocking a worker thread. Errors keep the server's own text through the same result[_, str] story as every other package. The protocol core is usable now; pooling, cluster routing and pub/sub are all here too. connect dials with a deadline, runs AUTH and SELECT , and hands back a Conn that any task may share -- one round trip at a time, serialized by an internal lock. do runs one command; a reply that violates the protocol breaks the connection for good, while a server-side command error only fails that call. Heavier use goes through Pool (shared connections with idle probing), Cluster (slot routing with MOVED/ASK handling and same-slot checks), explicit MULTI transactions on direct Conns, and pull-model pub/sub where the caller drives sub_next (a 4-line pump feeds a chan when push suits better). slang Copy import "redis" ; import "time" ; import "log" ; let dl = until_of (time. mono () + 5000000000 ); let cr = redis. connect ( "redis://:secret@cache.internal:6380/2" , dl); guard let c = cr else let e = err_of (cr) { log. error ( "connect: " + e); exit ( 1 ); } // encode a command to wire bytes (binary-safe values pass through) let wire : bytes = redis. encode ([ to_bytes ( "SET" ), to_bytes ( "k" ), to_bytes ( "v" )]); // run it; at most one command is ever in flight per Conn let r = redis. do (c, [ to_bytes ( "PING" )], dl); // decode one reply; ok(none) means feed more bytes and retry, // err means the bytes violate the protocol let dr: result [ opt [redis.Decoded], str ] = redis. decode ( wire ); // cluster hash slot of a key (0..16383), honouring {...} hash tags let s: int = redis. slot ( "{user1000}.following" ); // connection strings parse into Configs for pooling and clusters let ur = redis. parse_url ( "redis://alice:secret@cache.internal:6380/2" ); // pooled and clustered use underneath (see the table) let pr = redis. new_pool ( "redis://cache.internal:6380" , 8 ); redis. close (c); Function Signature redis.encode(args) bytes — one command as a RESP2 array of bulk strings redis.decode(buf) / redis.decode_at(buf, pos) result[opt[Decoded], str] — one reply plus bytes consumed redis.slot(key) int — cluster hash slot with {...} tag support redis.parse_url(url) result[Config, str] — redis:// / rediss:// redis.connect(url, deadline) / redis.connect_config(cfg, deadline) result[Conn, str] — dial, AUTH , SELECT redis.do(c, args, deadline) result[Reply, str] — one command round trip redis.close(c) / redis.usable(c) — shutdown / may commands still be attempted strings ping , echo , get , set , set_ex , set_nx , del_keys , exists , expire , pexpire , ttl , pttl , persist , incr , decr , incr_by , decr_by , append , strlen , mget , mset hashes hset , hget , hgetall , hdel , hexists , hkeys , hvals , hlen , hincr_by lists lpush , rpush , lpop , rpop , llen , lrange , ltrim , lindex , lrem sets sadd , smembers , srem , scard , sismember , spop sorted sets zadd , zrange , zrange_scores , zrank , zscore , zrem , zcard , zincr_by keys key_type , rename , rename_nx , scan ( KEYS omitted on purpose) pool new_pool , new_pool_config , acquire , release , pool_do , pool_close cluster new_cluster , cluster_do , cluster_refresh , cluster_close , c* typed wrappers, same-slot multi-key checks transactions multi , queue , exec , discard , watch , unwatch (direct Conns; pool and cluster routing stay out) scripting eval , evalsha with NOSCRIPT fallback pub/sub subscribe , sub_add , sub_next , sub_remove , sub_close (pull model; pump pattern in docs) streams xadd , xadd_maxlen , xrange , xrevrange , xlen , xtrim , xdel , xread , cluster cxadd / cxlen / cxread (groups deferred) A reply is a redis.Reply : kind is one of REPLY_SIMPLE , REPLY_ERROR , REPLY_INT , REPLY_BULK or REPLY_ARRAY , with the payload

title: regex
text: Regular expressions on str or bytes , matched by slang's own Thompson NFA — no external library, so a program that matches text stays as dependency-free as a plain TCP one. compile returns an opaque rawptr handle (freed with regex.free , like net.tls_* and sql ), and a bad pattern comes back as a descriptive result[rawptr, str] . Matching is linear time, always. There is no backtracking, so the classic catastrophic pattern (a+)+$ — which makes a backtracking engine take exponential time on a hostile input — runs in the same microseconds here as any other pattern. That is the point of choosing this engine for a server language: patterns and subjects both arrive from the network. The price is the RE2/Go one, and it is not negotiable: no backreferences and no lookaround . Both require backtracking; (?=...) and friends are a compile error, not a silent mis-parse. Function Signature regex.compile(pat) result[rawptr, str] regex.free(re) — regex.groups(re) int — number of capture groups regex.is_match(re, s) bool — s is a str regex.is_match_bytes(re, b) bool — b is bytes regex.find(re, s) / find_bytes(re, b) [int] regex.find_at(re, s, from) / find_bytes_at(re, b, from) [int] find returns byte offsets as [start, end, g1start, g1end, ...] , or an empty list when there is no match — so the result is GC-owned and there is no match handle to leak. find_at starts at an offset, which is how you walk every match. slang Copy import "regex" ; let cr = regex. compile ( "(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})" ); guard let re = cr else let e = err_of (cr) { log. error ( "bad pattern: " + e); // e.g. "missing ) at offset 9" exit ( 1 ); } if regex. is_match (re, "due 2026-09-09" ) { let m = regex. find (re, "due 2026-09-09" ); println ( to_str (m[ 0 ]) + ".." + to_str (m[ 1 ])); // whole match: 4..14 println ( to_str (m[ 2 ]) + ".." + to_str (m[ 3 ])); // year: 4..8 } regex. free (re); Supported: literals, . , classes [a-z] [^...] [[:digit:]] , escapes \d \D \w \W \s \S \b \B \A \z \xHH , quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} and their lazy ? forms, groups (...) and (?:...) , alternation | , anchors ^ $ . Matching is leftmost-first (Perl-style priority), and . does not match \n . Subjects are matched with an explicit length, so a bytes containing NUL matches correctly rather than stopping at the NUL — and \D matches a NUL byte like any other non-digit. Bounds, so a hostile pattern can't exhaust memory or stack: 4096 compiled instructions, 100 nesting levels, 32 capture groups, and {n,m} counts up to 1000. Each is a descriptive compile error, never a crash. A compiled regex is safe to share across tasks, and is meant to be: it carries a small pool of reusable match buffers, so concurrent matchers allocate nothing per match. Compiling is the expensive part (it is also the only part that grows the task stack) — compile once, match many times, ideally not once per request. Where this lands on speed. Measured single-threaded on ^(GET|POST|PUT) (/[a-z0-9/_-]*) HTTP/1\.([01])$ against a 26-byte subject, 200k iterations: engine matches/sec on (a+)+$ vs a hostile input slang regex ~721k 2µs, correct answer POSIX regexec ~372k fast here, but no limits PCRE2 (interpreted) ~2.4M 0.2s, then gives up ( MATCHLIMIT ) PCRE2 (JIT) ~8.6M same — JIT does not save it So: ~1.9x faster than libc's POSIX engine, and several times slower than PCRE2 on benign input — PCRE2's interpreter and especially its JIT are very good, and this is an honest gap. The trade is deliberate: on adversarial input the ordering inverts completely, because linear time is a guarantee here and a hope there. is_match is markedly cheaper than find (it binds no capture slots at all), so prefer it when you only need a yes/no. Matching scales with tasks — ~3.2M/sec across 16. Because matching never grows the task stack, regex is cheap to use per connection: 600 concurrently-live tasks each matching and then parking pe

title: s3
text: S3-compatible object storage, signed with AWS Signature Version 4: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO and the rest. slang Copy import "s3" ; import "proc" ; let r = s3. new_client ( "https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" , "eu-west-1" , access_key, secret_key); // or s3.from_env(proc.getenv): AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, // AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_REGION, S3_ENDPOINT guard let c = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } s3. put_object (c, "uploads" , "avatars/42.png" , png, "image/png" , deadline); // ok(etag) s3. get_object (c, "uploads" , "avatars/42.png" , deadline); // ok(bytes) s3. get_range (c, "uploads" , "logs/today" , 0 , 1023 , deadline); // first KiB s3. head_object (c, "uploads" , "avatars/42.png" , deadline); // ok(some(Object)) or ok(none) s3. delete_object (c, "uploads" , "avatars/42.png" , deadline); s3. list_objects (c, "uploads" , "avatars/" , "/" , "" , 1000 , deadline); // ok(Page); page.next continues s3. put_large (c, "backups" , "db.dump" , dump, "" , 16 * 1048576 , deadline); // multipart s3. presign_get (c, "uploads" , "avatars/42.png" , 900 ); // ok(url) for 15 minutes s3. presign_put (c, "uploads" , "incoming/x.bin" , 300 ); The payload is hashed into the signature ( x-amz-content-sha256 ), so a body altered in transit is refused by the server. Signing keys are cached for the day they belong to. Errors carry S3's own code and message ( s3: NoSuchKey: The specified key does not exist. ). Addressing and listing. Addressing is path-style by default ( endpoint/bucket/key ), which MinIO, R2 and most compatible stores want. Set c.path_style = false for virtual-host style ( bucket.endpoint/key ). list_objects returns up to 1000 keys a page in key order. Pass page.next to get the next page; with a delimiter, deeper keys fold into page.prefixes . Multipart. create_multipart , upload_part , complete_multipart and abort_multipart are the raw steps (every part but the last at least 5 MiB). put_large drives them, uploading in one request when the data fits in a part, and aborting if a part fails so no orphaned parts are left to be billed. Presigned URLs last 1 second to 7 days. presign_at signs at a given time, for tests and for URLs several servers must agree on. Google Cloud Storage speaks the same protocol through its XML API with HMAC keys (Cloud Storage settings, Interoperability): use s3.new_client("https://storage.googleapis.com", "auto", access_id, secret) . HMAC keys belong to a service account. For service-account JSON keys or the metadata server, use the separate dolphlabs/gcs package. title: sigv4
text: AWS Signature Version 4 for any service. s3 signs with it, and so do clients for SQS, SNS and the rest. slang Copy import "sigv4" ; let s = sigv4. new_signer (access_key, secret_key, "eu-west-1" , "sqs" ); s.session_token = token; // temporary credentials, or leave "" let h: map [ str ] str = {}; h[ "content-type" ] = "application/x-amz-json-1.0" ; h[ "x-amz-target" ] = "AmazonSQS.SendMessage" ; let amzdate = sigv4. amz_date_now (); // "20150830T123600Z" let auth = sigv4. sign (s, "POST" , "sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" , "/" , {}, h, sigv4. payload_hash (body), amzdate); // send Authorization: auth, X-Amz-Date: amzdate, the headers in h, and // X-Amz-Security-Token when there is a token let url_query = sigv4. presign (s, "GET" , host, "/" , {}, 900 , amzdate); sign signs the given headers plus host , x-amz-date and any security token. The signing key is derived once a day per signer and replaced as a whole, so a request never pairs one day's date with another day's key. derive_key , authorization and presign_query are the same steps for a caller that keeps its own key, as s3 does. uri_encode and canonical_query encode the way SigV4 signs. The tests use AWS's published test-suite vectors. Limits. Objects are read and written whole, in memory (or as one byte range). Redirects are not followed, since a redirect would change the host the signature covers. API # gc struct DayKey { date: str , key: bytes } stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:27 # The signing key for one day, held as one object so a request never pairs one day's date with another day's key while the day turns. gc struct Signer stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:29 # fn new_signer (access_key: str , secret_key: str , region: str , service: str ) -> Signer stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:40 # fn amz_date_now () -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:46 # "20130524T000000Z" for now, UTC. fn payload_hash (body: bytes ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:51 # The hex SHA-256 SigV4 signs as the payload hash. fn derive_key (secret_key: str , date: str , region: str , service: str ) -> bytes stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:57 # kSigning = HMAC(HMAC(HMAC(HMAC("AWS4" + secret, date), region), service), "aws4_request"). date is YYYYMMDD. fn signing_key (s: Signer, date: str ) -> bytes stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:65 # The signer's key for date , derived once a day. fn scope (date: str , region: str , service: str ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:75 # fn uri_encode (s: str , keep_slash: bool ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:96 # RFC 3986 percent-encoding as SigV4 wants it: everything but A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . ~ (and / in paths, when keep_slash). fn canonical_query (q: map [ str ] str ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:119 # Parameters encoded, then sorted by their encoded form: the order SigV4 signs and the order a request should send. fn authorization (access_key: str , key: bytes , region: str , service: str , method: str , path: str , query: map [ str ] str , headers: map [ str ] str , payload: str , amzdate: str ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:156 # The Authorization header for a request whose signed headers are exactly headers (which must hold host and x-amz-date, and x-amz-security-token with temporary credentials). For callers that keep their own key cache, as s3 does; most callers want sign . fn sign (s: Signer, method: str , host: str , path: str , query: map [ str ] str , headers: map [ str ] str , payload: str , amzdate: str ) -> str stdlib/sigv4/sigv4.sl:170 # The Authorization header for a request to host : signs headers plus host, x-amz-date and, with temporary credentials, x-amz-security-token. The caller sends X-Amz-Date (and the token) with the same values. fn presign_query (access_key: str , key: bytes , region: str , service: str , session_token: str , method: str , host: str , path: str , query: map [ str ] str ,

title: sort
text: Sorting lists in place with Go's sort engine shape, plus binary search over what is already sorted. ints , floats and strings sort by native comparison; by sorts any list of anything by a key function returning int , float or str ; by_stable keeps equal keys in their original order; the search functions binary-search a sorted list and answer opt[int] . slang Copy import "sort" ; let xs = [ 5 , 3 , 9 , 1 , 3 ]; sort. ints (xs); // in place, ascending let i = sort. search_ints (xs, 3 ) ?? - 1 ; let users = load_users (); sort. by (users, user_age); // key fn -> int, float or str sort. by_stable (users, user_name); // equal keys keep original order let names: [ str ] = []; for u in users { push (names, u.name); } sort. strings (names); let fs = [ 3.5 , 1.0 , 0.0 / 0.0 , 0.5 ]; sort. floats (fs); // NaN values sort first (Go's rule) The unstable sorts allocate nothing; each runs an entry pass that answers already-sorted and fully-reversed lists in one scan, and the quicksort settles each duplicate group in one partition pass, so four-valued million-element lists sort in tens of milliseconds. by_stable merges with one scratch list of about n/2 elements. API # fn ints (xs: [ int ]) -> [ int ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:41 # Sorts xs in place, ascending. Unstable. Answers an already-sorted or strictly descending list in one scan, and duplicate-heavy data in no more passes than its distinct values take to settle, so the whole call is allocation-free either way. fn floats (xs: [ float ]) -> [ float ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:56 # Same engine over floats, with a total order despite the type's own: NaN values sort before every number and equal to each other (Go's sort.Float64s rule), which is what makes the partition finite. fn strings (xs: [ str ]) -> [ str ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:70 # Same engine over strings, bytewise: "" sorts first, and the order is exactly what < gives — bytes, not locale, not Unicode points. fn by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn (T) -> K) -> [T] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:86 # Sorts xs in place by key, ascending. Unstable: when two keys are equal, which was first is whatever the comparisons fell into. A call is free to permute equal keys differently on a re-run, so anything whose output must not change between runs uses by_stable . fn by_stable[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn (T) -> K) -> [T] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:107 # Sorts xs in place by key, ascending, and equal keys keep their original order: an adaptive merge sort. Natural runs are kept (a strictly descending run is reversed, which keeps order for equal keys, since a strictly descending run has none), windows of 32 are insertion-sorted, and runs merge bottom-up taking the left on equal keys. Nearly-sorted data therefore costs about one comparison per element, not n log n. fn search_ints (xs: [ int ], v: int ) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:148 # The first index of v in xs, sorted ascending, or none. On a list which is not sorted the result is defined but useless; it never reads past the list. fn search_floats (xs: [ float ], v: float ) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:168 # Same contract over floats: that includes searching for NaN, which finds the first NaN and sorts first under sort.floats. The index found for a searched NaN is where the first NaN of the list sits. fn search_strings (xs: [ str ], v: str ) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:191 # Same contract over strings: the first index of an exactly equal string, bytewise as sort.strings orders them. fn search_by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn (T) -> K, v: K) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/sort/sort.sl:212 # Lower bound over a list already sorted by key: the first index whose key is not before v. Equality is !(a < b) && !(b < a) , which is == for int and str keys; for a float key it reads equal NaNs -- both raw comparisons false -- as a hit, the same reading by gives them.

title: sql
text: A SQLite driver (linked automatically, only when a program imports sql ). Connections and prepared statements are opaque rawptr handles, exactly like net.tls_* ; free them with sql.close / sql.finalize . Every fallible call returns result[_, str] whose error is SQLite's own message — no such table: users , near "SELCT": syntax error , UNIQUE constraint failed: users.id — so a bad query stays as visible as a bad socket read ( guard let … else let e = err_of(r) ), never a silent null . The column getters are infallible (SQLite coerces types; an out-of-range index is a programming error, returning 0 / "" ), so they return bare values. Function Signature sql.open(path) result[rawptr, str] — ":memory:" for in-memory sql.close(db) — sql.exec(db, sql) result[int, str] — runs statement(s), returns rows changed sql.last_insert_id(db) int sql.prepare(db, sql) result[rawptr, str] sql.finalize(st) — sql.reset(st) result[bool, str] — clears bindings, re-run sql.bind_int/bind_float/bind_text/bind_blob(st, idx, v) result[bool, str] — idx is 1-based sql.bind_null(st, idx) result[bool, str] sql.step(st) result[bool, str] — true = row ready, false = done sql.col_count(st) int sql.col_name(st, i) / col_text(st, i) str — i is 0-based sql.col_int(st, i) int sql.col_float(st, i) float sql.col_blob(st, i) bytes sql.col_is_null(st, i) bool slang Copy import "sql" ; import "log" ; let dr = sql. open ( "app.db" ); guard let db = dr else let e = err_of (dr) { log. error ( "db open: " + e); exit ( 1 ); } sql. exec (db, "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)" ); let pr = sql. prepare (db, "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id > ?" ); guard let st = pr else let e = err_of (pr) { log. error ( "prepare: " + e); // e.g. "no such table: users" exit ( 1 ); } sql. bind_int (st, 1 , 0 ); while true { let sr = sql. step (st); guard let more = sr else let e = err_of (sr) { log. error ( "step: " + e); break ; } if !more { break ; } println ( to_str (sql. col_int (st, 0 )) + " " + sql. col_text (st, 1 )); } sql. finalize (st); sql. close (db); SQLite calls block the worker — use them for real work off the accept loop (wrap in a spawn ed task), the same caveat as fs . One connection per rawptr ; there is no pool and no async stepping. For Postgres, see pg , which runs on the scheduler instead. Query complexity is capped per connection so SQLite's recursion stays inside the task stack: at most 50 terms in a compound SELECT ( UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT ) and an expression depth of 400 (roughly, terms in one AND / OR chain). SQLite's stock limits of 500 and 1000 allow a single legal query to want ~325KB of C stack, which would force a task stack far too fat to spawn per connection. Long IN lists, wide result sets, and recursive CTEs are not affected — they don't recurse. Exceeding a cap is a normal error through result[_, str] ( too many terms in compound SELECT ), not a crash. title: strings
text: Search, trim, case, split and join on str . The package cannot be named str because that token is the type — the same reason Go calls its own strings . slang Copy import "strings" ; strings. find ( "hello world" , "world" ); // 6, or -1 strings. rfind ( "a/b/c" , "/" ); // 3 strings. contains ( "hello" , "ell" ); strings. has_prefix ( "hello" , "he" ); strings. has_suffix ( "hello" , "lo" ); strings. count ( "a,b,c" , "," ); // 2 strings. hash ( "user:42" ); // a 64-bit hash, never negative: in-process only strings. trim ( " hi \r\n" ); // "hi" (space/tab/CR/LF) strings. trim_start (s); strings. trim_end (s); strings. to_upper ( "hi" ); strings. to_lower ( "HI" ); // ASCII only strings. slice ( "hello" , 1 , 3 ); // "el" strings. slice ( "hello" , - 3 , 5 ); // "llo" — negative counts back strings. repeat ( "ab" , 3 ); // "ababab" strings. replace ( "a,b,c" , "," , " | " ); strings. split ( "a,b,,c" , "," ); // ["a", "b", "", "c"] strings. join (parts, "," ); // the inverse of split strings. join_bytes (parts, b "," ); // the same for [bytes]: sized once, copied once strings. from_float ( 0.1 + 0.2 ); // "0.30000000000000004" strings. escape_html ( "<a href='x'>" ); // "&lt;a href=&#39;x&#39;&gt;" strings. escape_js ( "it's </script>" ); // "it\u0027s \u003c/script\u003e" escape_html writes & < > " ' as character references, which is safe in text and in a quoted attribute of either quote. escape_js makes the inside of a JavaScript string literal of any quote ( ' , " or a backquote), safe inside <script> and inside an attribute. Both return the input itself, with no allocation, when nothing needs escaping. template escapes every value through them. from_float returns the shortest text that to_float reads back as exactly the same number, as to_str , println , inspect and json.encode now do too (they used six significant digits, so to_str(123456789.125) was "1.23457e+08" ). The difference is the names: from_float writes NaN and the infinities as NaN , Infinity and -Infinity , where to_str writes nan , inf and -inf . This is a compiler-provided native package, and it has to be: str supports len , + and == and nothing else — it cannot be indexed or sliced — so none of it could be written in slang without converting to bytes and back on every call. byteutil covers the bytes side. Three behaviours worth knowing: Indices are byte offsets and the case operations are ASCII-only. str is UTF-8 bytes, and these are byte operations, which is what protocol text (header names, methods, config keys) wants. For text people type, use unicode : characters, case folding and normalisation. slice clamps rather than panics. Slicing is how you narrow a string you just searched, and a find that returned -1 on the line above should not turn the next line into a crash. A negative index counts from the end. split and join are exact inverses. Adjacent separators produce empty elements, so the result always has count(s, sep) + 1 elements and join(split(s, sep), sep) == s for any non-empty separator. An empty separator splits into single bytes. API # strings. find ( str , str ) -> int # strings. rfind ( str , str ) -> int # strings. contains ( str , str ) -> bool # strings. has_prefix ( str , str ) -> bool # strings. has_suffix ( str , str ) -> bool # strings. count ( str , str ) -> int # strings. hash ( str ) -> int # strings. trim ( str ) -> str # strings. trim_start ( str ) -> str # strings. trim_end ( str ) -> str # strings. to_upper ( str ) -&

title: tar
text: Archives in memory: read every entry of a zip (stored or deflated, ZIP64, UTF-8 names) or a tar (ustar, pax, GNU long names; a .tar.gz is compress.gunzip first), and write either. slang Copy import "tar" ; import "zip" ; let r = zip. open (data); guard let arc = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } for e in arc.entries { let pr = zip. safe_path (e.name); // refuses ../, /abs, C:\ (zip slip) guard let rel = pr else { continue ; } if !e.is_dir { let body = zip. read (arc, e); // inflated, size and CRC-32 checked } } let w = zip. new_writer (); w. add ( "report.csv" , csv_bytes, now_unix); // deflated, or stored if that is smaller w. add_stored ( "logo.png" , png, now_unix); let out = w. finish (); // result[bytes, str] let tr = tar. parse (tar_bytes); // result[[tar.Entry], str] let tw = tar. new_writer (); tw. add_file ( "bin/run.sh" , script, 493 , now_unix); // mode 0755 tw. add_symlink ( "current" , "releases/42" , now_unix); let tb = tw. finish (); Reading is checked against the archive itself. A zip is read from its central directory, as unzip does. Each entry's local header must be where the directory says, its data inside the archive, and no two entries may share bytes: overlapping entries are how a 40 KB zip claims petabytes. An entry inflates to at most the size the directory states, and must match it and its CRC-32. zip.Limits bounds one entry (256 MiB), all of them together (1 GiB) and their count. Every tar header's checksum is checked, and a size may be octal or GNU base-256. A pax header's path , linkpath , size , mtime , uid and gid override the ustar fields. Data past the end of the archive is an error, never a short entry. Encrypted zip entries and methods other than stored and deflate are listed but not read. Zip names must be UTF-8, so CP437 names are refused. Names are never trusted. Neither package touches the file system. safe_path gives back a relative, cleaned name, or an error for an absolute path, a .. segment, a drive letter, a backslash or a NUL. Check a tar symlink's target the same way before creating it. Writers refuse such names, and the same name twice. Times are Unix seconds. A zip's MS-DOS timestamp has no zone and 2-second steps; it is read as UTC, and the extended timestamp extra field wins when present. tests/archive_interop reads archives made by Python's zipfile and tarfile , Info-ZIP and bsdtar. What these writers write was checked with unzip -t , Python and bsdtar. title: template
text: HTML templates that escape each value for where it lands, and plain-text templates for email bodies and other text. The syntax is Go's ( {{ .field }} , if , range , with , define , pipelines), and so is the safety model: escaping is decided by the HTML around each action when the template is parsed, not by the caller remembering to escape. slang Copy import "template" ; gc struct Item { name: str , url: str , price: int } gc struct Page { title: str , items: [Item], user: str } let r = template. parse ( "page" , "<h1>{{ .title }}</h1>" + "<ul>{{ range $i, $it := .items }}" + "<li><a href=\"{{ $it.url }}\" title=\"{{ $it.name }}\">{{ add $i 1 }}. {{ $it.name }}</a></li>" + "{{ else }}<li>nothing yet</li>{{ end }}</ul>" + "<script>const user = {{ .user }};</script>" ); guard let t = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } // syntax and context errors, with line numbers let html = template. render (t, page); // result[str, str] template. add (t, "layout" , "<html><body>{{ template \"page\" . }}</body></html>" ); template. render_named (t, "layout" , page); let mail = template. parse_text ( "welcome" , "Hi {{ .name }},\n{{ range .items }}- {{ .name }}\n{{ end }}" ); Each action is escaped for its context: Where What the value becomes text, quoted attribute & < > " ' as character references URL attribute ( href , src , action , …), at the start only http , https , mailto , tel or a relative URL; anything else, javascript: above all, becomes about:invalid#blocked later in a URL percent-encoded ( /search?q={{ .q }} ) <script> , on* attributes a JavaScript literal (JSON), < > & ' as \u escapes inside a JS string escaped as string content, whatever the quotes <style> , style attributes letters, digits and # % . , - only, else ZgotmplZ Refused when the template is parsed: an action in a tag or attribute name, in an unquoted attribute value, in an HTML or JavaScript comment, and branches of an if or range that leave the HTML in different states ( {{ if .x }}<a href="{{ end }} ). {{ .html | raw }} writes trusted HTML unescaped in text, and escapes it anywhere else. Data is any value json.encode takes: a struct's fields are .name , a list ranges, a map's keys are fields (ranged in sorted key order). A missing field is an error, not an empty string, so a typo does not render as silence; use if , with or default for data that may be absent. Language. {{ if }} / {{ else if }} / {{ else }} , {{ with }} , {{ range }} (with $i, $x := and {{ else }} for empty), {{ $x := … }} and {{ $x = … }} with block scope, $ for the root, pipelines ( {{ .name | upper }} ), parentheses ( {{ len (index .items 0).tags }} ), {{/* comments */}} and {{- / -}} to trim whitespace, {{ define }} and {{ template "name" . }} (nested up to 64 deep). Functions: eq ne lt le gt ge , and or not (short-circuit, as Go's), len index default join upper lower trim add sub , print printf ( %s %v %d %f %.2f %q %x %t ), json urlquery raw . An unknown function or variable is a parse error. Cost. Parsing and escape analysis happen once; a Template is safe to render from many tasks at once. Rendering encodes the data with json.encode and indexes it with encoding.json_tape (one C pass, no allocation per value), resolves variables to slots at parse time, and escapes with strings.escape_html / escape_js , which return their input unchanged when nothing needs escaping. A 100-row table page (15 KB, six actions a row) rendered in 0.6–0.8 ms, against 1.0–1.2 ms for Go's html/template on the same page, run alternately on one machine. text: slang Copy import "time" ; let t0 = time. mono (); // monotonic clock; a `duration` (int64 ns) time. sleep ( 20000000 ); // sleep for a duration (ns) let elapsed = time. mono () - t0; // duration arithmetic let deadline = time. mono () + 5000000 ; // timeout math for net calls let wall = time. wall (); // unix epoch time in nanoseconds let d = time. http_date (); // "Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT", the current second time.put_http_date(w, off) writes the same 29 bytes into a wire and returns off + 29 (with a zero-length wire it only counts): what http uses for Date . For dates other than now, use timez . API # time. mono () -> duration # time. wall () -> int # time. sleep ( int ) # time. http_date () -> str # time. put_http_date ( wire , int ) -> int #

title: timez
text: Calendar time, written in slang on top of the native time clock: instants, dates, durations, text formats, time zones, test clocks and cron. Import "timez" . slang Copy import "timez" ; let t = timez. now (); // a Time: an instant, UTC println (t. rfc3339 ()); // 2026-10-13T09:30:15Z println (t. rfc3339_milli ()); // 2026-10-13T09:30:15.000Z (toISOString) println (t. http_date ()); // Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT println (t. format ( "%A %e %B %Y, %H:%M" )); // Tuesday 13 October 2026, 09:30 let r = timez. parse_rfc3339 ( "2026-10-13T11:30:15+02:00" ); // offsets applied let due = t. date (). add_months ( 1 ); // Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29 let ttl = timez. parse_duration ( "1h30m" ) ?? 0 ; // nanoseconds; "7d" works too println (timez. relative (t. add (- 3 * timez.MINUTE), t)); // 3 minutes ago let zr = timez. load_zone ( "Europe/Berlin" ); // the system's tz database guard let berlin = zr else let e = err_of (zr) { println (e); exit ( 1 ); } println (t. in_zone (berlin). format ( "%H:%M %Z" )); // 11:30 CEST let cr = timez. parse_cron ( "*/15 9-17 * * MON-FRI" ); guard let cron = cr else let e = err_of (cr) { println (e); exit ( 1 ); } let next = cron. next_after (t, berlin); // opt[Time], DST-aware Values. Time is Unix seconds plus nanoseconds, so it spans 0001-01-01 to 9999-12-31 and beyond. 64-bit nanoseconds stop at 1677-2262. Date is a calendar day: birthdays, due dates, report days. Durations are int nanoseconds, the unit time.sleep and deadlines take. Constants run from NANOSECOND to HOUR and DAY (24 hours). The calendar is proleptic Gregorian, with no leap seconds. Calendar. Fields: year() to nanosecond() , weekday() , year_day() , iso_week() , is_leap_year , days_in_month . Arithmetic: add(d) , sub(t) , and add_days , add_months and add_years , which clamp to the end of the month. Rounding and periods: truncate(d) , round(d) , and start_of_* and end_of_* for minute, hour, day, week (Monday), month and year. Comparing: before , after , equal , compare , min , max . Dates: days_until , and years_until , which counts an age by whether the anniversary has passed. Text. rfc3339 , rfc3339_milli , rfc3339_nano and rfc3339_at(offset) . parse_rfc3339 is strict: it refuses a timestamp with no offset, because one without names no instant. parse_date . http_date , and parse_http_date for all three forms RFC 9110 has recipients accept. rfc2822 and parse_rfc2822 . format(layout) : strftime directives, locale-free. parse_duration and format_duration , Go's format plus d . relative . Time zones. Loading. load_zone(name) reads the IANA database, from $ZONEINFO or /usr/share/zoneinfo . It follows each file's POSIX-TZ rule past its last transition, and refuses names that could reach other files. A missing database is an error that says how to install it, never a silent UTC. fixed_zone(name, offset) gives a zone at a fixed offset. Reading. t.in_zone(z) gives a ZonedTime : local fields, abbrev , is_dst , rfc3339 with the offset, and format with real %z and %Z . Local arithmetic. add_days , add_months and start_of_day work in local wall time, so a day across a DST change is 23 or 25 hours. Wall time to instant. zoned(z, y, m, d, h, mi, s, how) converts a local wall time to an instant. how decides the skipped and repeated hours: COMPATIBLE moves forward through a gap and takes the earlier of an overlap, as Temporal and java.time do. The others are EARLIER , LATER and REJECT . Operations. system_clock() / fixed_clock(t) : a Clock to pass in state, so tests advance and set the time instead of sleeping. start_stopwatch() , which measures on the monotonic clock. interval(a, b) : half-open, with contains , overlaps and intersection . deadline(t) gives the until that socket and channel calls take. parse_cron : five fields, names, steps and @daily macros. When both day fields are set, a day matches either (Vixie). next_after(t, zone) eval

title: toml
text: TOML v1.0.0: decode a config file into your own types, or convert it to JSON. slang Copy import "toml" ; struct Db { host: str , port: int , replicas: [ str ], timeout_ms: opt [ int ] } struct Config { name: str , db: Db } let r: result [Config, str ] = toml. decode (text); guard let cfg = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } // "toml: line 4: ..." toml. to_json (text); // result[str, str] decode is to_json then json.decode , so a document decodes into whatever JSON does: structs, gc struct s, lists, maps, opt (a missing key is none ) and enums, and an offset date-time into a timez.Time . Tables keep their keys in document order. Values in JSON. Strings, integers and booleans are the same JSON values. Floats are numbers, except inf and nan , which have no JSON form and become null , as json.encode writes them. An offset date-time is an RFC 3339 string with T and Z ( 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z , ...-07:00 ); local date-times, dates and times are strings as written. A string may hold U+0000 (as \u0000 ), though a slang str cannot. Strictness. All of TOML 1.0, and everything it forbids is an error naming the line: a key or table defined twice, a table extended after it was closed, an integer outside 64 bits, an invalid date, a control character in a string, a bare CR, invalid UTF-8. Nesting is limited to 256 levels. A subnormal float (below about 2.2e-308) is refused, as to_float refuses one. tests/toml_parity checks 748 documents against Python's tomllib : the spec's examples, one invalid document per rule, and seeded random and mutated ones. Cost. One pass over the bytes builds a tree that holds each value's JSON text, so nothing is decoded twice. A string with nothing to escape and a plain decimal integer are a single copy of their source. On a 1.1 MB document of 6,000 tables, to_json took about 220 ms against about 180 ms for Go's BurntSushi/toml decoding into map[string]any and about 550 ms for Python's tomllib (Linux container; ratios, the host was throttled). A config file of a few KB parses in microseconds. API # fn to_json (text: str ) -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/toml/toml.sl:85 # The document as JSON. fn decode[T](text: str ) -> result [T, str ] stdlib/toml/toml.sl:101 # The document decoded into T, as json.decode would decode its JSON.

title: unicode
text: Text as people write it: UTF-8 validation, characters rather than bytes, case-insensitive comparison and canonical normalisation, from the Unicode 18.0 tables. Use it for usernames, display names, length limits and search; strings stays the tool for protocol text. slang Copy import "unicode" ; unicode. valid (s); // strict UTF-8: no overlongs or surrogates unicode. valid_bytes (body); // the same check on bytes, before to_str unicode. count ( "café 😀" ); // 6 characters (len is 10 bytes) unicode. truncate (bio, 160 ); // first 160 characters, none split unicode. runes ( "aé" ); // [97, 233]: code points unicode. encode ( 0x1F600 ) ?? "" ; // "😀"; none for a surrogate or U+0000 unicode. fold ( "Straße" ); // "strasse": full case folding unicode. equal_fold ( "STRASSE" , "straße" ); // true unicode. nfc (name); // composed form: store and compare this unicode. nfd (name); // decomposed form unicode. is_nfc (name); // true when nfc(name) == name The same text can arrive as different bytes: é is one code point (U+00E9) from most keyboards and two ( e + U+0301) from some, so two strings that both display as café can compare unequal. Normalise with nfc at the boundary, before storing or comparing. For a case-insensitive key, such as a username that must be unique however it is capitalised, store unicode.nfc(unicode.fold(unicode.nfd(name))) , or compare with equal_fold , which implements the Standard's canonical caseless match (D145) and so treats "STRASSE" , "straße" and a decomposed spelling as equal. Invalid UTF-8 is repaired, not guessed at. The checks report it ( valid is false, is_nfc is false); every transform ( fold , nfc , nfd , truncate , runes ) replaces each malformed sequence with U+FFFD, as the Standard recommends, so its output is always valid UTF-8. Code that must reject bad input rather than repair it calls valid first. Cost. Native, reading each str in place. valid , valid_bytes , count , is_nfc and equal_fold allocate nothing on the GC heap, and fold , nfc , nfd and truncate return their input itself, with no allocation, when it is already in the requested form, which covers ASCII and nearly all real text. Long runs of combining marks are reordered in linear time, so hostile input cannot make normalisation quadratic. The tables add about 125 KB to a program that imports the package, and nothing to one that does not. Out of scope: compatibility normalisation (NFKC/NFKD, which maps ﬁ to fi and full-width letters to ASCII), grapheme clusters (a flag emoji or an accented letter can be more than one code point, and truncate counts code points), and locale-specific casing (Turkish dotted and dotless i). The tables come from the Unicode data files under the Unicode License v3. Its notice is compiled into every program that imports unicode , so the binary carries it wherever it goes; see THIRD_PARTY.md and LICENSES/Unicode-3.0.txt . title: uuid
text: UUIDs per RFC 9562: make version 4 (random) and version 7 (time-ordered), check, parse and convert. An id is a plain str in canonical form (36 characters, lowercase hex, hyphens at 8, 13, 18 and 23), the form JSON, logs and Postgres's uuid text already use, so it crosses those boundaries unconverted and has exactly one spelling to compare or key a map by. slang Copy import "uuid" ; let r = uuid. v7 (); guard let id = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); // only if the OS has no randomness } uuid. is_valid (id); // true: canonical form only uuid. version (id) ?? 0 ; // 7 uuid. time_ms (id) ?? 0 ; // unix ms it was made let p = uuid. parse ( "{0190F4E2-7C1A-7B3E-9F21-6C0D5A4E8B17}" ); // ok("0190f4e2-7c1a-7b3e-9f21-6c0d5a4e8b17"); also urn:uuid: and 32 hex let bad = uuid. parse ( "0190f4e2-7c1a" ); // err("uuid: want 36 characters (8-4-4-4-12 hex digits), got 13") Use v7 for anything stored, primary keys above all: its first 48 bits are the creation time in milliseconds, so ids sort by time and new rows append to an index instead of landing on random pages. Within one millisecond the order is random, because v7 keeps no state and any task may call it without a lock. v4 is 122 random bits and reveals nothing, not even when it was made. Both draw from crypto.rand , and return an error rather than an id from a weaker source. v7_at(unix_ms) stamps a given time (tests, ids that carry an event's time); to_binary and from_binary convert to and from the 16-byte form; uuid.NIL and uuid.MAX are the RFC's two special values. is_valid accepts any version and variant, so ids from Postgres's gen_random_uuid() or other services pass. API # let NIL = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" ; stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:36 # The nil and max UUIDs (RFC 9562 sections 5.9 and 5.10). let MAX = "ffffffff-ffff-ffff-ffff-ffffffffffff" ; stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:37 # fn v4 () -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:44 # A random UUID, version 4: 122 random bits. fn v7 () -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:56 # A time-ordered UUID, version 7, stamped with the current wall-clock time: 48 bits of unix milliseconds, then 74 random bits. fn v7_at (unix_ms: int ) -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:63 # A version 7 UUID stamped with unix_ms instead of the clock: for tests, and for ids that must carry an event's own time. Errors if unix_ms is negative or does not fit in 48 bits. fn is_valid (s: str ) -> bool stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:87 # Is s a UUID in canonical form: 36 characters, lowercase hex digits, hyphens at 8, 13, 18 and 23? Any version and variant passes, so ids made elsewhere (Postgres's gen_random_uuid, another service) are accepted. Upper case, braces and urn:uuid: are not: run those through parse . fn parse (s: str ) -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:109 # The canonical form of a UUID written any common way: canonical, upper or mixed case, in braces ({...}), as a urn:uuid: URN, or as 32 hex digits without hyphens. The error names the position and what was expected there. fn version (s: str ) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:119 # The version number of a canonical UUID (4 for v4, 7 for v7, 0 for NIL), or none if s is not canonical. fn time_ms (s: str ) -> opt [ int ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:129 # When a v7 UUID was made, in unix milliseconds. none if s is not a canonical version 7 UUID with the RFC 9562 variant: other versions keep no time, or keep it in another layout. fn to_binary (s: str ) -> result [ bytes , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:151 # The 16 bytes of a UUID, most significant first: the binary form databases store (Postgres uuid on the wire, a BINARY(16) column). Accepts every spelling parse does. fn from_binary (b: bytes ) -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/uuid/uuid.sl:156 # The canonical form of 16 bytes, the reverse of to_binary .

title: websocket
text: A WebSocket client (RFC 6455) over ws:// and wss:// , with permessage-deflate (RFC 7692) when asked for. In the Autobahn TestSuite's client run ( tests/live/websocket , 517 cases), 440 cases are OK, 3 INFORMATIONAL and 2 NON-STRICT, with no failures. The NON-STRICT two are invalid UTF-8 inside one frame, caught when the frame is whole rather than byte by byte. The 72 UNIMPLEMENTED are window-size variants of permessage-deflate this client does not offer. slang Copy import "websocket" ; let o = websocket. options (); o.protocols = [ "v2.chat" ]; // offered; Conn.protocol is the server's pick o.headers = [ "Authorization: Bearer " + token]; o.ping_every = 20000000000 ; // keepalive: a ping every 20 s o.compress = true ; // permessage-deflate let r = websocket. dial_with ( "wss://example.com/live" , o, deadline); guard let ws = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } websocket. send_text (ws, "{\"subscribe\":\"prices\"}" , deadline); websocket. send_binary (ws, frame, deadline); let mr = websocket. recv (ws, deadline); // result[opt[Message], str]; none: the deadline passed guard let got = mr else let e = err_of (mr) { panic (e); } guard let m = got else { return ; } if m.kind == websocket.Kind.Text { handle (websocket. text (m)); } websocket. close (ws, 1000 , "bye" , deadline); // the close handshake recv returns Text , Binary or Close messages, reassembled from their fragments. It answers pings and consumes pongs as they arrive, and answers the server's close before returning it. A deadline that passes loses nothing: the next recv carries on, even partway through a frame. One task reads at a time; any number may send, and a send is one whole frame written under a lock, so frames from different tasks never interleave. What it refuses. Masked or reserved-bit frames, unknown opcodes, fragmented or oversized control frames, lengths not in their shortest form, continuations with nothing to continue, text that is not UTF-8 (checked per fragment as it arrives), close codes a peer may not send, and messages over max_message (32 MiB by default, counted after inflation, so a compression bomb is cut off). Each fails the connection with the matching close code (1002, 1007, 1009). In the handshake: a wrong Sec-WebSocket-Accept , a subprotocol or extension that was not offered, and redirects. A redirect would send the handshake, and any credentials in it, somewhere the caller did not name. Keepalive. With ping_every set, a ping goes out each interval and a connection whose ping goes a whole interval unanswered is closed; recv then reports why. Pongs arrive through recv , so a connection nobody reads cannot keep itself alive. Compression is offered without context takeover in either direction. The server must accept server_no_context_takeover , so each message it sends inflates on its own. Each message this client sends is compressed on its own too, as a sync-flushed stream with no final block ( compress.deflate_raw_flush ), which a server keeping one decompressor for the whole connection reads correctly. No 32 KiB window per direction stays alive between messages. A message is sent compressed only when that makes it smaller. Text with U+0000. A str ends at its first zero byte, so websocket.text(m) stops there. m.data holds every byte, and send_text_bytes sends one. Frames are masked with keys drawn from a 4 KiB pool of crypto.rand bytes, refilled as it empties. A frame is built in one allocation by encoding.xor_mask . Large frames are read in chunks and joined once. title: x509
text: X.509 certificates: read them, check them, and make requests for them. slang Copy import "x509" ; let r = x509. parse_pem (pem); // result[[x509.Cert], str]: every CERTIFICATE block guard let certs = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } let c = certs[ 0 ]; c.common_name; c.dns_names; c.ip_addrs; // the subject and its subjectAltName entries c.not_after; // unix seconds x509. expires_in (c); // seconds left; negative once expired x509. matches_host (c, "www.example.com" ); // RFC 6125, SANs only let v = x509.Verify { roots_pem: "" , host: "api.example.com" , at: 0 , purpose: "server" }; x509. verify (certs, v); // ok(true), or why not let key = crypto. ecdsa_p256_private_to_pem (crypto. ecdsa_p256_generate () ?? b "" ) ?? "" ; let names = x509.Request { common_name: "api.example.com" , dns_names: [ "api.example.com" ], ip_addrs: [] }; x509. csr (key, names); // result[str, str]: PKCS#10, PEM x509. self_signed (key, names, 90 ); // result[str, str]: a certificate, PEM Cert holds der (exactly the bytes parsed), subject and issuer (RFC 4514, most specific first), common_name , serial (lowercase hex), not_before and not_after (unix seconds), dns_names , ip_addrs , emails and uris , is_ca and max_path_len (-1 when unset), key_usage ( digital_signature , key_encipherment , cert_sign , ...), ext_key_usage ( server_auth , client_auth , ...; others as dotted OIDs), key_type ( rsa , ec-p256 , ec-p384 , ed25519 , ...) and key_bits , public_key_pem (SPKI, which crypto's *_from_pem functions take), signature_alg and fingerprint (SHA-256 of der , lowercase hex). parse_der takes one certificate or several concatenated, as a TLS chain arrives. Names. matches_host and verify 's host follow RFC 6125: only subjectAltName entries count, never the subject CN (browsers and Go stopped trusting it); a wildcard is only the whole left-most label and stands for exactly one label; an IP literal matches IP entries, compared as addresses. Verifying. chain[0] is the leaf, the rest intermediates in any order. roots_pem is the trust anchors ( "" for the system's, loaded once and shared); at checks validity at a given time ( 0 for now); purpose is "server" , "client" or "" . A failure says why, in words that do not change with the OpenSSL version: certificate has expired , certificate is not yet valid , hostname mismatch , IP address mismatch , certificate is not for this purpose , certificate signed by unknown authority , self-signed certificate not in the roots , certificate signature does not verify , issuer is not a CA , path length constraint exceeded . Client identity (mTLS). With net.tls_ctx_require_client the handshake has verified the client's chain; read it with x509.parse_der(c.peer_certs()) on a link, or x509.parse_der(net.tls_peer_certs(ssl)) on a handle from net.tls_accept . x509 does not import net , so a program that only reads certificates does not link TLS. Making them. csr builds the PKCS#10 request an ACME server or any CA takes: the names, the public key, signed by the private key (RSA, EC or Ed25519 in PEM). self_signed makes a leaf for development TLS and tests: CA:FALSE, server and client auth, a random 128-bit serial, valid from now for 1 to 36500 days; verify it by passing its own PEM as the roots. Request needs a common name or at least one DNS name or IP. All the ASN.1 is OpenSSL's; the package parses no DER itself. Errors start with x509: . title: xml
text: XML 1.0 with namespaces, for the APIs that still speak it: SOAP, payment gateways, SAML, RSS and Atom, sitemaps. Parse into a tree, read it, write one back. slang Copy import "xml" ; let r = xml. parse (body); guard let doc = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } // "xml: line 3 col 9: ..." let title = doc. find ( "channel/title" ) ?? doc; // a path of local names for item in doc. find_all ( "channel/item" ) { println (item. child_text ( "link" )); } let env = xml. parse (soap) ?? doc; let body_el = env. child_ns ( "http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" , "Body" ); let out = xml. element ( "note" ). set_attr ( "id" , "7" ). add (xml. element ( "to" ). add_text ( "Ada & Bob" )); xml. write (out); // ok("<note id=\"7\"><to>Ada &amp; Bob</to></note>") A Node is an Element , Text , Comment or Pi ( n.kind ), with name as written, local , ns (the namespace URI), attrs , children and text . attr(name) , attr_ns(ns, local) , child(local) , child_ns , children_named , elements() , text_content() and child_text(local) read it. Adjacent text, CDATA and references are one Text node. Comments and PIs are dropped unless Limits.keep_comments . What it refuses. A DOCTYPE, by default: DTDs are how entity expansion ("billion laughs") and external entities (XXE) get in. Limits.skip_doctype skips one without an internal subset (old RSS feeds carry one), and an internal subset is always refused. Entities other than the five predefined ones and character references are refused, and so is anything not well-formed: mismatched tags, duplicate attributes, an unbound prefix, < in an attribute, ]]> in text, -- in a comment, a control character, content after the root. Encodings other than UTF-8 (and US-ASCII) are refused. Limits: 16 MiB, 256 levels, 1024 attributes on an element, a million nodes. Every error names the line and column. tests/xml_parity checks 64 documents against Python's expat: the same verdicts, and the same tree for the accepted ones (one deliberate difference: an ISO-8859-1 declaration). Writing escapes text and attribute values. A name that is not an XML name, a comment holding -- , or a control character is an err , never a broken document. Declare namespaces as attributes ( xmlns:p ). Cost. On a 3.5 MB RSS feed of 20,000 items, parse took 410-470 ms here, against about 150 ms for Go's encoding/xml into a generic tree and 89 ms for Python's ElementTree (C expat). Most of the gap is the collector tracing a large tree as it grows. Parse documents of that size off the request path. title: yaml
text: YAML 1.2 for configuration files: decode into your own types, or convert to JSON. slang Copy import "yaml" ; struct Db { host: str , port: int , replicas: [ str ], timeout_ms: opt [ int ] } struct Config { name: str , db: Db } let r: result [Config, str ] = yaml. decode (text); guard let cfg = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } // "yaml: line 4: ..." yaml. to_json (text); // result[str, str]: the stream's one document yaml. to_json_all (text); // result[[str], str]: every document (--- between them) let all: result [[Config], str ] = yaml. decode_all (text); decode is to_json then json.decode , so a document decodes into whatever JSON does: structs, gc struct s, lists, maps, opt (a missing key is none ) and enums. Mappings keep their keys in document order. to_json and decode take a stream of exactly one document (none reads as null ); to_json_all and decode_all take any number. What is read. Block and flow mappings and sequences; plain, single- and double-quoted scalars; literal ( | ) and folded ( > ) block scalars with chomping ( - , + ) and indentation indicators; comments; several documents ( --- , ... ); anchors ( &a ) and aliases ( *a ); merge keys ( <<: *base ); and the core tags ( !!str , !!int , !!float , !!bool , !!null , !!map , !!seq ). What is refused , as an error naming the line: other tags ( !custom , %TAG ), explicit keys ( ? key ), a mapping or sequence used as a key, a recursive alias, a duplicate key, and tabs in indentation. Plain scalars resolve by YAML 1.2's core schema, so yes , no , on and off are strings, not booleans as in YAML 1.1. null , ~ and an empty value are null; true / false (and True , TRUE , ...) are booleans; 12 , -3 , 0o17 and 0x1F are integers, which must fit 64 bits; 1.5 , .5 , 1e3 , .inf and .nan are floats, the last two null in JSON, as json.encode writes them. Anything else, dates included, is a string. A key's JSON name is its text, so 1: and "1": are the same key. Aliases share the node they name; writing the JSON expands them. Expanding to more than four times the document's own nodes (at least a million) is an error, so a few lines of nested aliases ("billion laughs") cannot blow up. Anchors belong to their document. Nesting is limited to 256 levels. Checked against ruamel.yaml (YAML 1.2) on 732 streams in tests/yaml_parity: config files and edge cases, invalid streams for each rule, and seeded random and mutated ones. Where ruamel departs from YAML 1.2 ( 1_000 and 0b101 as numbers, timestamps, tabs after key: ), this package follows the spec. Cost. One pass builds a tree of each value's JSON text; a one-line plain scalar, a quoted string without escapes and a plain integer are a single copy of their source. On a 1.1 MB document of 5,000 entries, to_json took about 230 ms against about 160 ms for Go's gopkg.in/yaml.v3 decoding into any (Linux container; ratios, the host was throttled). A config file of a few KB parses in well under a millisecond. API # fn to_json (text: str ) -> result [ str , str ] stdlib/yaml/yaml.sl:108 # The stream's one document as JSON: null if it has none, an error if it has more than one. fn to_json_all (text: str ) -> result [[ str ], str ] stdlib/yaml/yaml.sl:121 # Every document in the stream, as JSON. fn decode[T](text: str ) -> result [T, str ] stdlib/yaml/yaml.sl:150 # The one document decoded into T, as json.decode would decode its JSON. fn decode_all[T](text: str ) -> result [[T], str ] stdlib/yaml/yaml.sl:159 # Every document decoded into T.

title: zip
text: Archives in memory: read every entry of a zip (stored or deflated, ZIP64, UTF-8 names) or a tar (ustar, pax, GNU long names; a .tar.gz is compress.gunzip first), and write either. slang Copy import "tar" ; import "zip" ; let r = zip. open (data); guard let arc = r else let e = err_of (r) { panic (e); } for e in arc.entries { let pr = zip. safe_path (e.name); // refuses ../, /abs, C:\ (zip slip) guard let rel = pr else { continue ; } if !e.is_dir { let body = zip. read (arc, e); // inflated, size and CRC-32 checked } } let w = zip. new_writer (); w. add ( "report.csv" , csv_bytes, now_unix); // deflated, or stored if that is smaller w. add_stored ( "logo.png" , png, now_unix); let out = w. finish (); // result[bytes, str] let tr = tar. parse (tar_bytes); // result[[tar.Entry], str] let tw = tar. new_writer (); tw. add_file ( "bin/run.sh" , script, 493 , now_unix); // mode 0755 tw. add_symlink ( "current" , "releases/42" , now_unix); let tb = tw. finish (); Reading is checked against the archive itself. A zip is read from its central directory, as unzip does. Each entry's local header must be where the directory says, its data inside the archive, and no two entries may share bytes: overlapping entries are how a 40 KB zip claims petabytes. An entry inflates to at most the size the directory states, and must match it and its CRC-32. zip.Limits bounds one entry (256 MiB), all of them together (1 GiB) and their count. Every tar header's checksum is checked, and a size may be octal or GNU base-256. A pax header's path , linkpath , size , mtime , uid and gid override the ustar fields. Data past the end of the archive is an error, never a short entry. Encrypted zip entries and methods other than stored and deflate are listed but not read. Zip names must be UTF-8, so CP437 names are refused. Names are never trusted. Neither package touches the file system. safe_path gives back a relative, cleaned name, or an error for an absolute path, a .. segment, a drive letter, a backslash or a NUL. Check a tar symlink's target the same way before creating it. Writers refuse such names, and the same name twice. Times are Unix seconds. A zip's MS-DOS timestamp has no zone and 2-second steps; it is read as UTC, and the extended timestamp extra field wins when present. tests/archive_interop reads archives made by Python's zipfile and tarfile , Info-ZIP and bsdtar. What these writers write was checked with unzip -t , Python and bsdtar. sig: fn exec(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
text: Runs SQL with no parameters through the simple protocol, which accepts several statements separated by semicolons -- a migration, a schema. Returns the rows affected by the last statement. Rows a statement returns are read and discarded.  Never build `sql` from untrusted input: use query() and param

title: pg.stream
name: stream
sig: fn stream(c: Conn, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until) -> result[Rows, str]

title: pg.next_row
name: next_row
sig: fn next_row(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
text: Reads the next row of a stream into `rows` (at index 0). Returns false once there are no more; rows.affected and rows.tag are set then.

title: pg.stream_close
name: stream_close
sig: fn stream_close(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
text: Ends a stream early. The server is asked to cancel the query first -- and that request is seen through before the rest is drained, so it can never land on a LATER query on this connection -- then whatever it had already sent is read and dropped. The connection is then free.

title: pg.copy_in_start
name: copy_in_start
sig: fn copy_in_start(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
text: Starts COPY ... FROM STDIN. Send data with copy_in_send, then finish with copy_in_end -- or copy_in_abort, which rolls the COPY back.

title: pg.copy_in_send
name: copy_in_send
sig: fn copy_in_send(c: Conn, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
text: Sends COPY data. It need not end on a row boundary; the server reassembles it. An error in the data is reported by copy_in_end.

title: pg.copy_in_end
name: copy_in_end
sig: fn copy_in_end(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
text: Ends the COPY. Returns the number of rows loaded, or the server's error about the data -- in which case nothing was loaded.

title: pg.copy_in_abort
name: copy_in_abort
sig: fn copy_in_abort(c: Conn, reason: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
text: Abandons the COPY: the server discards everything sent. Ok once the server has confirmed; its "COPY from stdin failed" is the expected answer, not an error.

title: pg.copy_from
name: copy_from
sig: fn copy_from(c: Conn, sql: str, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
text: COPY ... FROM STDIN in one call. Returns the rows loaded.  pg.copy_from(c, "COPY users (id, email) FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv)", to_bytes("1,a@example.com\n2,b@example.com\n"), dl)

title: pg.copy_out_start
name: copy_out_start

title: pg.copy_out_next
name: copy_out_next
sig: fn copy_out_next(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[opt[bytes], str]
text: The next piece of COPY output -- in text and CSV formats, one row -- or none when it is complete.

title: pg.copy_to

text: COPY ... TO STDOUT in one call, buffered (up to the 256 MiB result limit; stream a larger one with copy_out_start / copy_out_next).

A timestamp without a time zone names no instant and is read as UTC, a

title: pg.release
name: release
text: Returns a connection to the pool: to the oldest waiting task if there is one, else to the idle list. One that is broken, closed, or still inside a transaction is closed instead, and its slot passed on: handing an open transaction to the next caller would run its statements inside someone else's unco

title: rand.Rng
name: Rng
text: A random number generator. Make one with `new` or `from_os`.

title: rand.new
name: new
text: A generator whose sequence is fixed by `seed`. Every int is a good seed, 0 and -1 included: splitmix64 spreads it over all 256 bits of state.

title: rand.from_os
name: from_os
text: A generator seeded from the operating system's CSPRNG, for when runs should differ (load generators, sampling in production). Its outputs are still predictable from earlier ones: this is not a source of secrets.

title: rand.fork
name: fork
text: A new generator seeded from `r`, for handing to a spawned task. Seeded parents give seeded children, so a whole run still replays from one seed. `r` advances by one step.

title: rand.next_u64
name: next_u64
text: The next 64 random bits.

title: rand.below
name: below
sig: fn below(r: Rng, n: int) -> int
text: An int in [0, n), each value equally likely. Panics if n is not positive: there is no int to return, as with an index out of range.

title: rand.between
name: between
sig: fn between(r: Rng, lo: int, hi: int) -> int
text: An int in [lo, hi], both ends included, each value equally likely. Panics if lo > hi. The full range, between(r, MIN, MAX), works.

title: rand.unit
name: unit
text: A float in the unit interval [0, 1): one of 2^53 evenly spaced values, so every float it returns is exact and 1.0 never appears.

title: rand.chance
name: chance
sig: fn chance(r: Rng, p: float) -> bool
text: True with probability `p`. p at or below 0 (or NaN) is never, p at or above 1 is always.

title: rand.shuffle
name: shuffle
text: Reorders `xs` in place, every order equally likely (Fisher-Yates).

title: rand.pick
name: pick
text: One element of `xs`, each equally likely; none if `xs` is empty.

title: rand.backoff
name: backoff
sig: fn backoff(r: Rng, attempt: int, base: int, cap: int) -> int
text: How long to wait before retry number `attempt` (0 for the first retry): a uniform draw from [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)], the "full jitter" strategy. Spreading over the whole interval, not just its top, is what stops a crowd of clients that failed together from retrying together. Units are whatev

title: rand.jitter
name: jitter
sig: fn jitter(r: Rng, d: int, frac: float) -> int
text: `d` scaled by a uniform factor in [1 - frac, 1 + frac]: jitter(r, d, 0.1) lands within 10% of d. frac is clamped to [0, 1] (NaN counts as 0), so the result is never negative. A d at or below 0 gives 0.

title: redis.REPLY_SIMPLE
name: REPLY_SIMPLE
text: The five RESP2 reply types. A reply is always one of exactly one.

title: redis.REPLY_BULK
name: REPLY_BULK
sig: let REPLY_BULK = 3; // $len\r\n<bytes> (bulk holds it, none when nil)

title: redis.Decoded
name: Decoded
text: A decoded reply plus how many bytes of the input it consumed, so a connection holding a read buffer knows what to keep.

title: redis.encode
name: encode
text:
Encode one command invocation as a RESP2 array of bulk strings: SET key value  ->  *3
$3
SET
$3
key
$5
value
 Takes already-encoded argument bytes, so binary-safe values pass through untouched. Pure: no I/O, no allocation beyond the result.

title: redis.decode
name: decode
text: Decode one RESP2 reply from the front of `buf`. ok(none) means the buffer ends mid-message -- feed more bytes and retry. ok(some(d)) consumed d.consumed bytes; anything after them is the next message. err means the bytes violate the protocol: never retry on the same connection.

title: redis.decode_at
name: decode_at
sig: fn decode_at(buf: bytes, pos: int) -> result[opt[Decoded], str]
text: Decode one reply starting at `pos` instead of 0, for readers that keep one long-lived buffer and an offset into it (see Conn): no slicing, so no per-recv copy of everything already buffered. consumed counts from `pos`.

title: redis.slot
name: slot
text: The hash slot of a key, 0..16383. `{...}` hash tags force colocation: only what sits between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed. Empty tags hash the whole key, and a `{` with no `}` is literal.

title: redis.parse_url
name: parse_url
text: Parse redis://[[username:]password@]host[:port][/db][?sslmode=...]. rediss:// forces sslmode=require. Percent-escapes in credentials and database decode the same way pg's URLs do.

title: redis.Conn
name: Conn
text: One server connection: exactly one round trip in flight at a time, serialized by lock. A Conn is safe to share between tasks; every public call below takes the lock for its whole exchange.

title: redis.connect_config
name: connect_config
sig: fn connect_config(cfg: Config, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
text: Open a connection from a parsed Config and run the handshake (AUTH when a password is set, SELECT when db is not 0). The deadline covers everything: DNS, TCP connect, TLS upgrade, login.

title: redis.connect
name: connect
sig: fn connect(url: str, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
text: Open a connection from a URL. See parse_url for the shape.

title: redis.do
name: do
sig: fn do(c: Conn, args: [bytes], deadline: until) -> result[Reply, str]
text: Run one command: args[0] is the command name. Exactly one reply is consumed, so at most one command is ever in flight per Conn; hold no lock of your own -- this takes c.lock for the round trip. Refused inside MULTI: queued commands answer +QUEUED, which no typed shape could read -- use queue there.

title: redis.close
name: close
text: Shut the connection down. In-flight calls on other tasks finish (or hit their own deadlines) first; close waits for the lock.

title: redis.usable
name: usable
text: True while commands may still be attempted: not closed, not broken. A server-side idle close is discovered on use, which marks the connection broken then.

title: sort.ints
name: ints
text: Sorts xs in place, ascending. Unstable. Answers an already-sorted or strictly descending list in one scan, and duplicate-heavy data in no more passes than its distinct values take to settle, so the whole call is allocation-free either way.

title: sort.floats
name: floats
text: Same engine over floats, with a total order despite the type's own: NaN values sort before every number and equal to each other (Go's `sort.Float64s` rule), which is what makes the partition finite.

title: sort.strings
name: strings
text: Same engine over strings, bytewise: `""` sorts first, and the order is exactly what `<` gives — bytes, not locale, not Unicode points.

title: sort.by
name: by
sig: fn by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]
text: Sorts xs in place by key, ascending. Unstable: when two keys are equal, which was first is whatever the comparisons fell into. A call is free to permute equal keys differently on a re-run, so anything whose output must not change between runs uses `by_stable`.

title: sort.by_stable
name: by_stable
sig: fn by_stable[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]
text: Sorts xs in place by key, ascending, and equal keys keep their original order: an adaptive merge sort. Natural runs are kept (a strictly descending run is reversed, which keeps order for equal keys, since a strictly descending run has none), windows of 32 are insertion-sorted, and runs merge bottom-

title: sort.search_ints
name: search_ints
text: The first index of v in xs, sorted ascending, or none. On a list which is not sorted the result is defined but useless; it never reads past the list.

title: sort.search_floats
name: search_floats
text: Same contract over floats: that includes searching for NaN, which finds the first NaN and sorts first under sort.floats. The index found for a searched NaN is where the first NaN of the list sits.

title: sort.search_strings
name: search_strings
text: Same contract over strings: the first index of an exactly equal string, bytewise as `sort.strings` orders them.

title: sort.search_by
name: search_by
sig: fn search_by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K, v: K) -> opt[int]
text: Lower bound over a list already sorted by key: the first index whose key is not before v. Equality is `!(a < b) && !(b < a)`, which is `==` for int and str keys; for a float key it reads equal NaNs -- both raw comparisons false -- as a hit, the same reading `by` gives them.

title: zip.safe_path
name: safe_path
text: A name made safe to join under an extraction directory: relative, with no "..", no drive letter or backslash, no NUL. A trailing "/" is kept. err names what is wrong; extracting such a name is how an archive writes outside the directory ("zip slip").

title: zip.Writer.add
name: Writer.add
sig: fn add(self: Writer, name: str, data: bytes, modified: int) -> Writer
text: Adds a file, deflated (stored instead when deflating does not make it smaller). `modified` is Unix seconds.

title: zip.Writer.add_stored
name: Writer.add_stored
sig: fn add_stored(self: Writer, name: str, data: bytes, modified: int) -> Writer
text: Adds a file as is: for data that is already compressed.

title: zip.Writer.add_dir
name: Writer.add_dir
sig: fn add_dir(self: Writer, name: str, modified: int) -> Writer
text: Adds a directory; "/" is appended to the name when missing.

title: zip.Writer.finish
name: Writer.finish
text: The whole archive, or the first problem an add ran into.
